title: 2026 ED138
text:
' is a large trans-Neptunian object (TNO) and possible dwarf planet in the classical Kuiper belt. It was discovered by Matthew Holman on 13 October 2026, while searching through Vera C. Rubin Observatory data taken earlier that year.
With an absolute magnitude of about 2.9–3.2, it is the brightest TNO found since Chiminigagua in 2013, the ninth- or tenth-brightest known TNO, and the brightest known object in the Solar System without a directly measured size. Its diameter is likely between 600 and 1000 km, potentially making it among the largest known dwarf planet candidates. Despite its brightness, it had long evaded detection due to a notably southern declination and being located near the crowded Galactic plane.
Little is known about its physical characteristics. It is moderately red, indicating that it likely has an icy surface darkened by organic material such as tholins.
Discovery
was discovered by Matthew Holman on 13 October 2026, while searching through Vera C. Rubin Observatory data taken earlier that year. The search made use of a computer program that Holman co-developed with Kevin Napier to automatically identify moving objects in images. Upon discovering , Holman recognized that it was unusually bright (apparent magnitude 20) and prompted further searches of earlier images. Mario Jurić uncovered 20 more Rubin images of  going back to 4 March 2026, while the B612 Asteroid Institute uncovered images taken by the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) from 2016 to 2019. With over 10 years of collected observations, the Minor Planet Center (MPC) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory team jointly announced the discovery of  on 27 October 2026.
On the day after the announcement, the MPC reported earlier observations taken by the Chilean VISTA telescope from 2010 to 2011. One day after that, the MPC reported even earlier observations found in Digitized Sky Survey images from 1937 to 2000. The earliest of these precovery observations was taken from Boyden Observatory in South Africa. With over 88 years of recorded observations (spanning 31% of its orbital period),  has the longest observation arc of any trans-Neptunian object besides Pluto.
was found in a region of sky close to the plane of the Milky Way, where it is crowded with stars. Even though it is among the brightest known trans-Neptunian objects, it had evaded detection for a long time because it is often obscured by background stars and its location has not been frequently observed by telescopes. The discovery of  was made possible by the Rubin Observatory's frequent monitoring of the entire southern celestial hemisphere and the use of computer algorithms for searching Rubin's large dataset.

Name
is the provisional designation of this object, given by the Minor Planet Center upon announcing its discovery. The provisional designation includes the year of the object's discovery (2026), the half-month of its discoverer's first observation date (E = first half of March), and the order of its discovery after other minor planets found during this half-month (D138 = 3,454th minor planet discovered). Minor planets eventually receive a permanent catalog number once their orbits are sufficiently known to be recoverable, a criterion that  has already passed. It is only after receiving a permanent number that minor planets can be named.
is a classical trans-Neptunian object. The International Astronomical Union gives these types of objects mythological names, preferably those associated with creation myths.
Orbit
is a trans-Neptunian object (TNO), orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune at an average distance of 43 AU. It resides in the Kuiper belt, where many other TNOs and dwarf planets like Pluto are found. It follows an elliptical and tilted orbit with an eccentricity of 0.14 and an inclination of almost 25° with respect to the ecliptic. These orbital characteristics make  a "hot" classical Kuiper belt object, which implies that it was disturbed from its original orbit through gravitational interactions with Neptune.
In its elliptical orbit,  approaches within 37.1 of the Sun at perihelion and strays as far as 49 from the Sun at aphelion. It takes roughly 283 years for  to complete one orbit around the Sun. This is close to  of Neptune's orbital period, meaning  might be in a weak 7:12 mean-motion orbital resonance with Neptune, like the dwarf planet Haumea. Despite having similar orbits,  is likely not related to Haumea and its family due to their different surface colors. as of October 2026, it is at a distance of roughly 46 from the Sun. It last came to perihelion in April 1926, and will return to perihelion in April 2209.

Physical characteristics
The diameter of  has not been measured but is inferred to be between 600 and 1500 km based on the object's absolute visual magnitude of 3.19 per Rubin Observatory estimates. A study led by Joseph Murtagh found an absolute magnitude of 3.11 using different means. The JPL Small-Body Database estimates the object's absolute magnitude as 2.85 based on potentially faulty color corrections. With an absolute magnitude of 3.19,  would be the tenth brightest known TNO in terms of absolute magnitude, between  and Ixion. With an absolute magnitude of 3.11 or 2.85, it would be the ninth, between  and Chiminigagua.
The unknown diameter of  stems from its unknown albedo or reflectivity: if it has a dark surface, it should be at the large end of its estimated size range, whereas if it has a bright surface, it should be at the small end.{{efn|The relationship between a Solar System body's diameter (D), albedo (p), and absolute magnitude (H) is mathematically written as D = \frac{1329 \mathrm{km}}{\sqrt{p}} \times 10^{-0.2H} (see Absolute magnitude#Solar System bodies (H)). What this equation shows is that the diameter must be small if the albedo is high, and conversely the diameter must be large if the albedo is low.}} Icy bodies in the upper end of this size range are expected to be rounded by their gravity, so  is a dwarf planet candidate—potentially among the largest known. Furthermore, its shape is likely to be approximately spheroidal. Its minimum likely diameter (at H = 3.27 and albedo = 0.25) would be comparable to that of Eris' moon Dysnomia, while its maximum diameter (at H = 2.39 and albedo = 0.04) would approach that of Eris. If its albedo were 0.10, seen in several large TNOs, and H = 3.19, its diameter would be 970 km, comparable to that of Ceres. A diameter between 610 and 970 km (H = 3.19 and albedo = 0.25–0.10) is considered likely.
Regardless of its size,  is unlikely to hold an atmosphere containing either methane, carbon monoxide, or nitrogen because it would entirely escape from its surface over the age of the Solar System. The theoretical albedo limit for retaining carbon monoxide is
